newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds close weaker after curve steepens.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds close weaker after curve steepens.

text.p: Canadian long bonds closed weaker on Friday after short-term bonds benefited from a stable Canadian currency and the yield curve steepened, analysts said.
"Not a bad performance at the front end in part because of (the Canadian dollar,)" said senior economist Mark Chandler for Goldman Sachs Canada.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond fell C$0.22 to C$115.20 to yield 6.760 percent, while its U.S. counterpart fell 8/32 to yield 6.44 percent.
The spread between the two narrowed to 32 basis points from 33 basis points at Thursday's close.

Canada's dollar closed today at C$1.3407 (US$0.7459) after opening at C$1.3391 (US$0.7467). In recent trading the unit weakened to a level of C$1.3450 (US$0.7435), but investors wondered if it would continue to rally after reaching C$1.3263 (US$0.7540) in early November.
"A quiet trading session because (there was) not a lot of economic information. That's likely to extend next week," Chandler said.
"Everybody's sitting pretty," agreed CIBC Wood Gundy Securities fixed income analyst Daniel Kelly.
Today the Bank of Canada conducted a round of reverse repurchase agreements at 2.75 percent to confirm its target range of 2.75-3.25 percent for the overnight rate.

The community-based corporation which runs the Vancouver airport set two Vancouver Airport Bonds today. The C$150 million 10-year 6.55 percent coupon bond had a price of C$99.985 and yielded 6.552 percent, 43 basis points over the 2006 Government of Canada bond.

The 30-year C$150 million 7.375 percent coupon bond was priced at C$99.784 to yield 7.393 percent, 60 basis points over the 2025 9.0 percent Government of Canada bond. The lead manager for both bonds was CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc.
In other prices, the Government of Canada's 7.0 percent of 2006 rose C$0.03 to C$106.43 to yield 6.131 percent. The U.S. 10-year bond fell 1/32 to yield 6.14 percent.
The negative spread between the two widened marginally to one basis point from zero at Thursday's close.
Canada's three-month cash bill traded at 2.83 percent against the U.S. bill at 5.16 percent.
